report.source_text: On the examination, there were bilateral cranial neuropathies involving trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII) and hypoglossal (XII) nerves. Lateral gaze was restricted bilaterally and there was bilateral upper and lower facial weakness with impaired eyebrow raise, eye closure and inability to smile. Weber’s test lateralised to the left ear and Rinne’s test demonstrated air conduction greater than bone bilaterally. Tongue was weak but midline on protrusion. Sensation was decreased to light touch and pinprick in V2 distribution on the right side. The remained of the neurological examination was unremarkable. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Early syphilitic meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 37-year-old woman with recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes and morbid obesity presented with a 2-week progressive neurological syndrome characterized by disequilibrium, unsteadiness, difficulty closing both eyes, right lip numbness, sequential bilateral hearing impairment, and slurred speech. She reported unprotected sexual contact and denied a primary syphilitic chancre. Neurological examination revealed bilateral cranial neuropathies involving CN V (decreased sensation in V2 distribution right), CN VI (restricted lateral gaze bilaterally), CN VII (bilateral facial weakness with impaired eye closure), CN VIII (bilateral hearing loss with Weber test lateralizing to left), and CN XII (tongue weakness). CSF analysis demonstrated lymphocytic pleocytosis (76% lymphocytes, 0.441×10⁹/L), elevated protein (1.28 g/L), normal glucose (CSF 3.8 mmol/L, serum 5.4 mmol/L), and normal opening pressure (13.5 cm H₂O)—consistent with aseptic meningitis. Serum serology confirmed active syphilis with positive TPPA, positive CMIA IgG and IgM, and RPR titer 1:32. MRI brain with gadolinium demonstrated enhancement of the trigeminal nerve at the pons and facial and vestibulochlear nerves at the geniculate ganglion, consistent with cranial nerve involvement in neurosyphilis. The constellation of clinical, CSF, serological, and neuroimaging findings established the diagnosis of early neurosyphilis with meningitis and multiple cranial neuropathies.
